manifest.name: go2_rl_gym
manifest.description: Built-in Go2 PPO training backend based on legged_gym and rsl_rl. This adapter calls the already-provisioned GPU-side go2_rl_gym scripts and copies the latest checkpoint into the platform run directory for the generic worker.

entrypoints.eval: bash -lc 'set -euo pipefail; load_run=$(cat {run_dir}/go2_run_name.txt); ckpt_name=$(basename {ckpt}); checkpoint=$(printf "%s\n" "$ckpt_name" | sed -E "s/[^0-9]*([0-9]+).*/\1/"); export PATH=/root/miniconda3/bin:$PATH; export PYTHONPATH=/opt/isaacgym:/opt/go2_rl_gym:${PYTHONPATH:-}; cd /opt/go2_rl_gym; python {repo}/apply_robot_spec.py --spec "${PLATFORM_ROBOT_SPEC:-}" --gym /opt/go2_rl_gym; python legged_gym/scripts/eval_once.py --task=go2_moe_cts --num_envs=8 --steps=16 --experiment_name=go2_moe_cts_platform --load_run="$load_run" --checkpoint="$checkpoint" --headless'
entrypoints.export: bash -lc 'set -euo pipefail; load_run=$(cat {run_dir}/go2_run_name.txt); ckpt_name=$(basename {ckpt}); checkpoint=$(printf "%s\n" "$ckpt_name" | sed -E "s/[^0-9]*([0-9]+).*/\1/"); onnx_dir=$(dirname {onnx_out}); onnx_name=$(basename {onnx_out}); mkdir -p "$onnx_dir"; export PATH=/root/miniconda3/bin:$PATH; export PYTHONPATH=/opt/isaacgym:/opt/go2_rl_gym:${PYTHONPATH:-}; cd /opt/go2_rl_gym; python {repo}/apply_robot_spec.py --spec "${PLATFORM_ROBOT_SPEC:-}" --gym /opt/go2_rl_gym; PLATFORM_ONNX_DIR="$onnx_dir" PLATFORM_ONNX_NAME="$onnx_name" timeout 240 python {repo}/export_history_onnx.py --task=go2_moe_cts --headless --experiment_name=go2_moe_cts_platform --load_run="$load_run" --checkpoint="$checkpoint"; test -s {onnx_out}'

notes: History-buffer ONNX export is implemented for browser sim2sim.

tasks.name: Wheel-Leg MoE-CTS
tasks.description: Four-frame MoE-CTS velocity tracking for W1W and standardized uploaded 16-DoF wheel-leg robots.

notes: The source snapshot is verified before GPU execution.
Every wheel-leg robot uses the same runtime reward and control profile; only URDF and robot-specific controls are injected.
Negative early reward totals are preserved; only terminal penalties remain negative by design.
Forward and reverse commands use symmetric sampling and the same velocity-tracking rewards from the first iteration.
Uploaded robots use the validated 203 Go2 terrain distribution and initial terrain difficulty.
Uploaded robots use an accelerated upright-height curriculum during the first 500 iterations.
Uploaded robots terminate episodes when roll or pitch exceeds the safe posture envelope.
Uploaded robot joint axes, non-wheel limits, and default-angle signs are preserved from the source URDF.
Evaluation requires forward-speed tracking error within 0.4 m/s.

manifest.name: wheel_leg_high_speed
manifest.description: High-speed MoE-CTS training for standardized 16-actuator wheel-leg robots. Flat, smooth-slope, and rough-slope terrain use a performance-driven symmetric command curriculum up to 8 m/s, with no periodic gait or active foot-lift objective.

notes: The policy uses the same explicit four-frame interface as the standard wheel-leg algorithm.
Forward and reverse speed commands expand together from 1 m/s to 8 m/s only after both directions meet the tracking threshold.
The linear tracking reward keeps the standard low-speed signal and uses 1 + 2.5 * max(cbrt(abs(vx_command)) - 1, 0) above 1 m/s.

tasks.name: Wheel-Leg High-Speed MoE-CTS
tasks.description: Performance-driven no-gait wheel velocity tracking on flat, smooth-slope, and rough-slope terrain for standardized 16-DoF wheel-leg robots.

notes: The source snapshot is verified before GPU execution.
Flat terrain occupies 50 percent of the terrain mix; smooth and rough slopes each occupy 25 percent.
Smooth slopes are capped at a 0.18 grade; rough slopes are capped at a 0.12 grade with +/-0.02 m surface variation.

Terrain tracks are 40 m long. Twelve terrain columns keep the total heightfield size equal to the proven 24 m profile, and finite-map edges end the environment as a timeout before the robot can fall off the mesh.
Flat, smooth-slope, and rough-slope terrain can reach X commands of +/-8 m/s, Y commands of +/-1 m/s, and yaw commands of +/-2 rad/s.
Reflex, phase-clock, air-time, swing-clearance, and stair-ascent rewards are disabled.
Above 1 m/s, the reward target progressively suppresses lateral and yaw authority with a quadratic curve; at 8 m/s it rewards straight-line motion even when raw Y/yaw joystick commands are non-zero.
On high-speed terrains, forward and reverse commands use identical sampling and high-speed-weighted tracking rewards.
Above 1 m/s, the PPO tracking reward and curriculum score use a sub-linear speed-dependent tolerance; low-speed behavior is unchanged and the 8 m/s criterion is stricter than version 0.5.0.
Above 1 m/s, a 2.5 gain is applied to the excess cube-root command-speed bonus while the 0-1 m/s tracking reward remains unchanged.

User-facing reward scales are used directly; explicit speed-conditioned multipliers gradually strengthen height tracking to 3x and vertical damping to 2x at 8 m/s, with no iteration-based reward schedule.
Link mass, center of mass, gains, motor strength, friction, and pushes use a narrow high-speed warm-up distribution; the default added base payload is -1 to 3 kg.
High-speed command, achieved speed, tracking error, height error, and vertical velocity diagnostics are emitted in the training metrics.
The velocity command curriculum uses the harmonic mean of forward and reverse quality, with per-direction safety floors, so small directional noise cannot permanently block promotion.
The curriculum promotes or demotes one level from measured tracking quality; training iteration never selects the level.
Wheel joints have no hard velocity limit; only configured motor torque envelopes remain active.
Uploaded robot motor envelopes remain the physical torque-speed limit.

manifest.name: wheel_leg_gait_rl_gym
manifest.description: Independent gait-switch MoE-CTS training for standardized 16-actuator wheel-leg robots. The gait clock is exposed to the policy and sampled per episode, while the underlying wheel-leg control and reward profile remains shared across uploaded robots.

notes: The server-matched gait runtime uses an explicit 10-frame MoE-CTS history.
Gait is introduced after ordinary locomotion pretraining and reaches an episode probability of 0.25.
The gait clock period is 0.7 seconds and is disabled/zeroed when the switch is off or the terrain requires free foothold selection.
Sim2Sim uses the same 60-dimensional observation order and phase progression.

tasks.name: Wheel-Leg Gait MoE-CTS
tasks.description: Ten-frame MoE-CTS velocity tracking with a 0.7-second light-unload gait curriculum that reaches 25% of episodes.

notes: The source snapshot is verified before GPU execution.
Every wheel-leg robot uses the same gait runtime; only URDF and robot-specific controls are injected.
The actor observes 57 base values followed by [sin(phase), cos(phase), gait_enabled]; motor temperatures are not actor inputs.
The critic observes 323 privileged values and the student history is 10 frames (600 flattened values).
Gait Barrier policy weight is 0.02; ordinary walking remains the dominant objective.
Gait sampling stays at 0% through iteration 1000, then ramps to 5% at 1500, 15% at 3000, and 25% at 5000.
Each diagonal unload lasts about 0.08 seconds and wheel-bottom clearance is bounded to 1-3 cm, preventing point-foot-like high stepping and leg folding.
Gait-on and gait-off episode length, tracking, and total reward are logged separately so aggregate metrics cannot hide a failed switch branch.
Gait phase and Barrier shaping are applied on wave/slope/rough-slope/flat only; stairs and obstacles receive the neutral gait suffix and retain free foothold selection.
Barrier advantages, policy loss, and value loss exclude gait-off and unsupported-terrain transitions instead of normalizing zero rewards into false gradients.
Gait-enabled episodes randomize which diagonal pair starts first, preventing a persistent first-leg bias.
Forward and reverse commands remain symmetric and gait is not command-gated.

Command sampling follows the go2_rl_gym reference — direct yaw-rate sampling without heading mode, five-second holds, zero-command and limit-velocity curricula, and per-terrain ranges where stairs match the obstacles range.
Stairs use the same difficulty curriculum as every other terrain (shared step-height curve, fixed 0.31 m tread); no dedicated stair friction, stair rewards, or stair command envelope exist.
Uploaded robot joint axes, non-wheel limits, and default-angle signs are preserved from the source URDF.
Incomplete or excessive collision shard sets are replaced by one complete per-link visual proxy before PhysX asset loading.

manifest.name: wheel_leg_jump_rl_gym
manifest.description: Independent MoE-CTS walk-and-jump training for standardized 16-actuator wheel-leg robots. A binary command triggers a finite jump, while vx, vy and yaw retain ordinary walking behavior when the command is off.

notes: The 16-DoF mixed position/wheel-velocity controller remains unchanged.
Initial jump training uses flat terrain only.
The binary jump command is observed in every actor frame.
Flight, apex and landing follow Omni-Jump task concepts without adopting its 12-DoF network ABI.

upstream.name: go2_rl_gym_wheel_leg_with_omni_jump_task_design
upstream.license: Bundled go2_rl_gym and rsl_rl components retain their MIT/BSD-3-Clause licenses. Omni-Jump is GPLv3 and is referenced for task-level concepts only; no Omni-Jump source code is bundled.

tasks.name: Wheel-Leg Jump MoE-CTS
tasks.description: Normal wheel-leg velocity tracking plus an explicit one-shot jump command on flat terrain.

notes: Actor input is 57 locomotion values, 16 motor temperatures, and [sin(jump_phase), cos(jump_phase), jump_command].
Critic input is 323 values; the 10-frame actor history is flattened to 760 for ONNX.
Jump episodes are sampled with probability 0.25 and trigger repeatedly every 2-4 seconds; the other 75 percent remain ordinary walking episodes.
Each binary jump command stays high for a randomly sampled 0.5-1.0 seconds.
After a 0.3 second preparation window, each wheel still touching is penalized until the first all-wheel flight event.
The first all-wheel flight event earns a one-shot bonus and every airborne control step earns cumulative flight reward.
All jump-specific rewards are zero when the binary command is off.
Uploaded robot axes, joint limits and calibrated motor envelopes remain robot-owned.

manifest.name: wheel_leg_hip_degradation
manifest.description: Hip-degradation robust MoE-CTS training for standardized 16-actuator wheel-leg robots. Half of episodes simulate one or more independently weakened hip motors without exposing the fault state to the policy.

notes: W1W uses the explicit four-frame policy interface from the 203 training source.
Hip degradation does not add actor, critic, or history observations.
Each episode has a 50% degradation gate; selected hips are capped at 40% to 90% of rated maximum torque (up to 60% degradation).
Straight-command foot-cycle shaping applies on every terrain and preserves a physical diagonal support pair.

The dedicated long flat track accepts only paired FL-RR or FR-RL lift events formed within 0.12 seconds, rejects unpaired lifts, enforces a 1.2-second pair cadence, and keeps each wheel center beneath its thigh axis.
Only the dedicated 30-second flat-track scenario samples forward commands from 0 to 3 m/s; mixed terrains retain their original symmetric curriculum and terrain-specific caps.
Heavy-payload foot-cycle shaping increases only above 10 kg of actual sampled payload and is capped at 2x by 20 kg.
Under heavy payload, an extra bounded term targets the single most-overdue foot instead of amplifying every foot.
A cadence-neutral completion bonus is limited to the least-completed feet so one leg cannot farm the reward.
A 0.35-second first-contact grace period prevents a never-supported wheel from escaping the cycle penalty.
Sim2Sim uses the W1W robot asset and mixed position/velocity control.

manifest.name: wheel_leg_gait_hip_degradation
manifest.description: Independent gait-switch MoE-CTS training for standardized 16-actuator wheel-leg robots. Hip motor degradation is disabled while the historical task id and policy observation ABI remain available for checkpoint resume.

notes: The server-matched gait runtime uses an explicit 10-frame MoE-CTS history.
Gait is enabled independently per episode with probability 0.25.
On continuous terrain, the 0.7-second gait clock remains active at zero command whenever the episode gait switch is enabled.
Stairs and discrete footholds emit the neutral gait suffix [0, 1, 0], while Sim2Sim applies the same terrain-dependent gait gate without changing the 60-dimensional observation order.
Hip degradation is hard-disabled; legacy continuation snapshots carrying the former sampling fields are accepted but ignored.

tasks.name: Wheel-Leg Gait Full-Torque MoE-CTS
tasks.description: Ten-frame MoE-CTS with a 0.7-second diagonal gait clock and a reset-safe 1.4-second cumulative yaw-drift check; gait shaping is limited to continuous terrain so stairs retain unconstrained foothold selection without changing the policy ABI.

notes: The source snapshot is verified before GPU execution.
Every wheel-leg robot uses the same gait runtime; only URDF and robot-specific controls are injected.
The actor observes 57 base values followed by [sin(phase), cos(phase), gait_enabled].
The critic observes 307 privileged values and the student history is 10 frames (600 flattened values).
Gait Barrier policy weight is 0.10, reduced from the server baseline 0.15.
Standard and gait-Barrier returns terminate at every actual episode reset.
Forward and reverse commands remain symmetric; an enabled gait switch advances the phase even at zero command and a disabled switch emits [0, 1, 0].
Gait phase is active only on wave, smooth slope, rough slope, and flat; stairs and discrete footholds emit [0, 1, 0] and receive no gait, Barrier, or clearance shaping.
Barrier advantages, statistics, policy loss, and value loss exclude every transition outside the active continuous-terrain gait branch.
Gait-enabled training episodes randomize their initial half-cycle, preventing a persistent first-moving diagonal; gait-off episodes still emit [0, 1, 0].
The gait Barrier uses diagonal pair-worst aggregation on continuous terrain only, preserving freedom to place feet on stairs and obstacles.

The cumulative yaw-drift reward compares wrapped actual heading change with the integrated yaw command over two gait cycles (1.4 s at the 0.7 s default period); it is reset-safe, command-aware, and uses a Huber transition at 0.2 rad.
The yaw-drift window is maintained outside the actor and critic observations, so the 60-dimensional observation and 10-frame history ABI remain unchanged.
Up-stair curriculum promotion requires six climbed risers and a normal episode timeout; falls cannot promote a stair level.
Stairs-up uses the normal per-terrain command ranges; no special x-only, positive-speed, lateral, or yaw restriction is applied.
Stair tread width is fixed at 0.31 m for every curriculum level.
Stairs-up receives the forward feet-air-time reward at scale 3.0; every other terrain receives exactly zero from that term.
Stairs-up now occupies 35% of environments, while stairs-down occupies 7% and the pure flat track remains 30%.
Stair ascent combines measured height rate with a short commanded-direction look-ahead toward the next riser, symmetrically for positive and negative X commands.
Stair/gait telemetry reports per-foot clearance, air duty, maximum clearance, and diagonal clearance RMS without entering observations or rewards.
Stand-nice applies only when gait is disabled and vx, vy, and yaw commands are all within 0.02; Hip, Thigh, and Calf each contribute one third and wheel joints are excluded.
The lin_vel_z curriculum retains a 0.3 damping floor; terrain weights are 1.0 on flat/smooth slope, 0.5 on wave/rough slope, and 0 on stairs and discrete footholds.
Pitch angular velocity adds -0.05 at full weight on continuous terrain, quarter weight on stairs, and zero weight on other discrete obstacles; there is no global pitch-angle constraint.
Ordinary flat samples vx in [-3, 3] m/s, vy in [-0.5, 0.5] m/s, and yaw in [-2, 2] rad/s with the normal five-second multi-axis cadence.

Half of ordinary-flat episodes instead hold one symmetric forward/reverse vx magnitude sampled uniformly from 0.3 to 3 m/s for the complete episode; no slope or rough-slope episode is forced into this subset.

A flat-only posture term ramps from zero at 2 m/s to full strength at 3 m/s and penalizes projected pitch plus body-height error equally for forward and reverse commands; stairs and obstacles receive exactly zero from it.

Training logs expose independent roll/pitch angle and angular-velocity RMS plus base vertical-speed and height-error RMS, with pitch groups by terrain and gait state; diagnostics do not enter reward or observations.
Flat diagnostics additionally report 0-1/1-2/2-3 m/s command-bin fractions and 2-3 m/s posture/tracking RMS split by gait on/off and forward/reverse direction.
Sparse terrain/gait diagnostic groups are aggregated only when present, so missing groups neither fail training nor appear as artificial zeros.
Four-GPU runs start with symmetric vx in [-1, 1] m/s, expand to [-2, 2] at iteration 1500, and reach [-3, 3] at iteration 4000; stairs-up follows its normal per-terrain ranges.
Teacher and deterministic-student rollouts each occupy 50% of the training environments, so stair telemetry reflects the exported policy more directly.
Termination reward is forced to -50 after uploaded robot settings are read; legacy specifications carrying zero cannot disable the fall penalty.
Built-in and uploaded robots randomize base COM independently on x/y/z within [-0.03, 0.03] m.
Hip degradation is forced off at config injection and again inside the runtime; old task and robot snapshots cannot reactivate it.
Every Hip retains 100% of its normal dynamic/thermal torque limit before ordinary motor-strength randomization.
The 60-dimensional observation, 10-frame history, task id, optimizer state and checkpoint tensor shapes are unchanged from version 0.1.9.
Uploaded robot joint axes, non-wheel limits, and default-angle signs are preserved from the source URDF.
